questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Reading by Shape While the Letter Names Are Unavailable
questions.learningObjective: Identify the reading route that operates without letter-name access
questions.stem: A translator's notes describe a reader who names words by their overall shape even when letter names are unavailable

options.text: The reader uses the direct lexical route bypassing letter names
The reader uses the phonological route to sound out each letter
options.misconception: confuses shape reading with phonological decoding

options.text: The reader relies on semantic guessing from context only
The reader uses sublexical grapheme-to-phoneme rules
options.misconception: confuses whole-word recognition with rule-based reading

questions.explanation: Reading by overall shape without letter-name access indicates the direct lexical route. Phonological and sublexical routes depend on letter-level processing, and pure semantic guessing ignores the visual form.
questions.hint: Shape-based reading bypasses letter names

questions.topic: Language: Reading by Shape While the Letter Names Are Unavailable
questions.learningObjective: Interpret preserved shape reading with impaired letter names

stimulus.body: A translator's notes report a reader who reads familiar words by shape with 90 percent accuracy but cannot name individual letters; nonword reading is at chance.

questions.stem: A translator's notes report shape reading 90 percent with chance nonword reading

options.text: Both reading routes are fully intact
Semantic memory is entirely lost
The phonological route is preserved and the lexical route is impaired
options.misconception: reverses the preserved and impaired routes

options.text: The direct lexical route is preserved and the phonological route is impaired

questions.explanation: High familiar-word accuracy with chance nonword reading indicates a preserved direct lexical route and an impaired phonological route. Both intact, reversed, and semantic-loss accounts do not fit.
questions.hint: Nonword reading needs the phonological route

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Reading Regular Words Correctly and Irregular Ones Wrongly
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise surface dyslexia into a route account
questions.stem: A translator's notes synthesise a reader with good regular and poor irregular word reading; propose an account

answer.exemplar: The reader relies on the sublexical phonological route, which succeeds on regular words but fails on irregular ones; the direct lexical route that stores irregular spellings is impaired

questions.explanation: Good regular and poor irregular reading indicates reliance on the sublexical phonological route, which succeeds on regular words but fails on irregular ones. The direct lexical route storing irregular spellings is impaired.
questions.hint: Regular success plus irregular failure is surface dyslexia

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: What Is Not Settled by the Presence of a Reading Difficulty
questions.learningObjective: Identify a reading difficulty's non-implications
questions.stem: A translator's notes ask which is not established by a reading difficulty alone

options.text: That a specific brain lesion is present
That reading performance is below expected
options.misconception: confuses the definition with its implications

options.text: That the person struggles with text
That intervention may be needed
options.misconception: infers action from a single observation

questions.explanation: A reading difficulty establishes impaired reading performance but not a specific brain lesion. Struggle and possible intervention are reasonable; neuroanatomical claims are not.
questions.hint: Symptoms do not locate lesions

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Lighter Boundary in One Community and Not in Another
questions.learningObjective: Compute the boundary shift between two communities
questions.stem: A translator's notes give boundary wavelengths of 520 nm in community A and 540 nm in community B; what is the shift
questions.explanation: The shift is 540 minus 520, which equals 20 nm. Community B's boundary sits 20 nm higher than community A's.
questions.hint: Subtract the lower wavelength from the higher

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: The Strong Form of the Language and Thought Claim
questions.learningObjective: Identify a prediction of the strong language-thought claim
questions.stem: A translator's notes ask what the strong language-thought claim predicts

options.text: All humans reason identically regardless of language
options.misconception: states the opposite of the strong claim

options.text: Language has no effect on nonverbal tasks
Speakers of different languages should show different thought patterns
Grammar is purely decorative and meaningless

questions.explanation: The strong claim predicts that speakers of different languages show different thought patterns. Identical reasoning, no effect, and decorative grammar are inconsistent with it.
questions.hint: Strong claim means different languages, different thoughts

questions.topic: Language: Evidence About the Language and Thought Claim That Is Hard to Interpret
questions.learningObjective: Design a study clarifying language-thought evidence
questions.stem: A translator's notes ask for a design that separates language effects from cultural effects

answer.exemplar: Test speakers of different languages who share a culture, or the same language across cultures, and compare nonverbal reasoning; a language effect should appear only where language differs

questions.explanation: Testing speakers of different languages sharing a culture, or the same language across cultures, and comparing nonverbal reasoning isolates language effects from cultural ones. A language effect should appear only where language differs.
questions.hint: Hold culture constant while varying language

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Signal That Carries Nothing Unless the Receiver Has a Rule
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a signal with no receiver rule

stimulus.body: A translator's notes report that a signal is presented to receivers lacking the matching decoding rule, and that their responses are at chance; receivers with the rule respond above chance.

questions.stem: A translator's notes report chance responses without the decoding rule

options.text: The signal carries information regardless of the receiver
The rule is irrelevant to information
The signal is physically undetectable
The signal carries information only with the matching rule

questions.explanation: Chance performance without the rule and above-chance with it shows the signal carries information only with the matching decoding rule. Physical detectability and rule irrelevance are ruled out.
questions.hint: The rule gates information

questions.topic: Language: What a Sign Used Without a Receiver Is Not Evidence Of
questions.learningObjective: Design a study of one-sided sign use
questions.stem: A translator's notes ask for a design testing whether a sign constitutes communication

answer.exemplar: Compare sign production with and without a receiver present, measure whether production rate changes with receiver availability, and test whether receivers respond appropriately

questions.explanation: Comparing sign production with and without a receiver, measuring rate changes, and testing receiver responses directly tests whether the sign constitutes communication. Communication requires bilateral uptake.
questions.hint: Vary receiver presence and measure uptake
